Tidal locking, the phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, profoundly shapes planetary climates. This gravitational handshake with its star forces one hemisphere into perpetual daylight while the other endures eternal night, creating some of the most exotic climate regimes in the universe.

The most dramatic consequence is the permanent temperature divide. The dayside of a tidally locked planet, particularly those orbiting red dwarf stars, can reach scorching temperatures exceeding 2,000°C on close-in worlds, while the nightside plummets toward absolute zero. Without rotation to distribute heat evenly, this stark contrast would seem to doom such worlds to habitability.

Yet atmospheres and oceans can rescue these planets from climatic extremes. On worlds with substantial atmospheres, winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, moderating both extremes. Climate models of planets like Proxima Centauri b suggest that with sufficient atmospheric pressure, the terminator zone—the twilight band between day and night—could maintain temperate conditions potentially suitable for life. Oceans, if present, provide even more efficient heat transport, potentially keeping the nightside above freezing.

Tidal locking also drives unusual atmospheric dynamics. The permanent dayside heating creates a climate engine that generates persistent winds flowing from day to night sides, with return flows aloft. On some worlds, this circulation can produce a standing wave pattern, with a permanent eye of hurricane-like storms at the substellar point.
